final_note: Brown is flavour — but past brown is bitter.

concepts.def: Starch breaks down to dextrins, browns in dry heat.
Amino acids and sugars brown in dry heat.
Sugar browns when heated above about 170 °C.
Cooking by dry heat in an oven.
Browning bread or grain by dry heat.
Browned dry outer layer of cooked food.

walkthroughs.body_html: Dextrinisation turns starch into shorter dextrins under dry heat, giving the golden colour and toasty flavour of toast, pastry crust and breadsticks. No protein is needed — this is purely a starch reaction.

The Maillard reaction needs amino acids and sugars together in dry heat. It creates the rich brown crust on roast meat, the colour of seared steak and the flavour of baked bread crust. It accelerates above about 140 °C.

Pure sugar starts to caramelise around 170 °C. It melts, browns and develops nutty, bittersweet flavours. Push past about 200 °C and it burns — pure bitterness. Caramelisation needs only sugar, not protein.
